hints: Look at each cell type in the table and ask yourself, will this cell still divide by mitosis many more times in an autoimmune response?

Remember telomerase is only useful where telomeres would be lost by repeated mitosis, so think about which cells are terminally differentiated and short lived versus long lived cells that undergo clonal expansion again and again.
walkthrough:
**Recall what telomerase is for**

Think simply. Every time a cell copies its DNA for mitosis, the ends of chromosomes (telomeres) get a little shorter. Telomerase rebuilds them.

So the rule is: only cells that will divide many, many times need active telomerase.

**Sort the cells into dividers and non-dividers**

Mature B-lymphocyte plasma cells are terminally differentiated factories. They make lots of antibody but they do not divide further.

Neutrophils are also terminally differentiated phagocytes. They are short lived, do not divide, and die after fighting pathogens.

Helper T-lymphocyte memory cells are different. They are long lived and must divide rapidly by mitosis to form a clone every time the self antigen appears in autoimmunity.

**Match to the table**

Plasma cells: no future mitosis, so no active telomerase, cross (X).

Neutrophils: no future mitosis, so no active telomerase, cross (X).

Helper T memory cells: repeated mitotic cycles ahead, so need active telomerase, tick.

That is X, X, tick, which is row C.

options.A: Incorrect because plasma cells and neutrophils do not divide further, so they would not need active telomerase to protect telomeres.
options.B: Incorrect because it gives telomerase to the two non-dividing cell types and removes it from the memory cells that actually need repeated mitosis.
options.C: Correct because only the helper T-lymphocyte memory cells will undergo many more mitotic cycles in chronic autoimmunity and so need active telomerase.
options.D: Incorrect because neutrophils do not divide and do not need telomerase, while plasma cells also lack future division.
